questions.question: What is an emergency fund for?

choices.label: Your car insurance payment that's due next month
A car repair you need to get to work
Concert tickets that are on sale this week

questions.explain: It's for urgent costs you couldn't plan for. A bill you know is coming belongs in your budget, and a sale is a want, not an emergency.

questions.question: Your housing and meal plan are paid through financial aid. What should you count as monthly essentials?

choices.label: Rent and meals anyway, to be safe
Only what you still pay each month, like phone and transportation

questions.explain: Count what you still pay yourself. Prepaid costs don't need to come out of your fund.

questions.question: What's a good first goal for an emergency fund?

choices.label: Six months, since smaller amounts don't really help
Whatever's left at the end of the month

questions.explain: One month is a realistic place to start and covers many common surprises. Every bit helps, and you can build toward three or six months later.

questions.question: Where is a good place to keep your emergency fund?

choices.label: In checking, so it's easy to reach
In a separate high-yield savings account
In an index fund, since it can grow more

questions.explain: A separate savings account keeps it from being spent by accident. Investments can drop in value right when you need cash.

questions.question: What matters most when choosing where to keep it?

choices.label: It's insured by the FDIC (banks) or NCUA (credit unions)
It has the highest rate you can find, even if it isn't insured
It gives you a bonus for opening the account

questions.explain: Insurance protects your money, up to the legal limit, even if the institution runs into trouble. A higher rate or a bonus doesn't matter if the money isn't safe.
